entities.description: Identify the active project and distinguish project-scoped resources.
entities.title: Find your project

entities.explanation_markdown:
# Find your project

Estimated time: 8 minutes, including four practice exercises.

Before starting, you should be comfortable with shell commands, arguments and
exit status, and know how a container image differs from a running container.
If these are unfamiliar, practice those basics before entering a cluster lab.
This is a bounded OpenShift pilot, not the complete DO180 course.

An OpenShift project gives your work a namespace. Deployments, Pods, Services
and Routes belong to that scope. Nodes belong to the cluster and are shared
infrastructure; they are not yours to reconfigure. Namespace access is not
cluster administrator access.

The lab supplies an assigned project and a scoped identity. Treat that assignment
as authoritative. `oc whoami` identifies the authenticated user; `oc project -q`
prints the selected project. Those answer different questions. Before changing
anything, compare the selected project with your assignment. Use `oc project
practice-a` only when `practice-a` is the project actually assigned to you.
The names in these exercises are examples, not authority to access another project.

Most namespaced commands use the selected project unless you supply another
namespace explicitly. An empty `oc get pods` result can simply mean you selected
the wrong project. It is not evidence that all applications disappeared from the
cluster. Likewise, a Forbidden response is an access boundary, not a request to
obtain administrator credentials. Check your assignment and ask for lab support
if the supplied access is broken.

Practice identifying scope before diagnosing resources. The useful habit is:
read the assignment, confirm the current project, then inspect that project's
resources. Do not use all-namespace queries or modify shared cluster resources
for these lessons.

entities.description: Use workload state, events and logs to support a diagnosis.
entities.title: Explain a workload symptom

entities.explanation_markdown:
# Explain a workload symptom

Estimated time: 10 minutes, including four practice exercises.
Prerequisite: Find your project.

A useful diagnosis joins a symptom to evidence. Start with `oc get pods` in the
assigned project. Read readiness, status and restart information separately.
A Running pod can still be unready; a process having started does not establish
that it can serve requests.

For a named pod, `oc describe pod web-example` shows conditions and events.
Replace the example with the actual pod name in a live lab. Events can explain
why a container did not start: an unavailable image, admission restriction or
scheduling problem calls for a different response than a crashing process.
For a started container, `oc logs deployment/web` can supply application evidence.
Do not expect useful application logs from a container that has never started.

Suppose a new pod shows ImagePullBackOff. That status means pulling its image is
failing with retries; it does not identify the cause by itself. If the events
say a tag does not exist, compare the Deployment image reference with the approved
image supplied by the lab. If instead the registry or network is unavailable,
report an infrastructure problem. Do not mark the learner wrong for an outage.

Record the observation before changing the workload. Repeated deletion or
restarts can remove useful context and will not repair a bad pod template.
After a repair, repeat the relevant observations and check the current rollout.

The text exercises accept only the command forms they request. They do not
execute a shell or recognize every equivalent spelling. The practical checkpoint
will be assessed by resource state and behavior rather than command history.

entities.description: Identify a failed rollout and select a repair that restores the desired workload.
entities.title: Deploy and repair a workload

entities.explanation_markdown:
# Deploy and repair a workload

Estimated time: 12 minutes, including four practice exercises.
Prerequisite: Explain a workload symptom.

A Deployment describes a desired set of application pods. Its controller uses
ReplicaSets to reconcile actual state with that desired state. Deleting a pod
does not delete that intent: the controller normally creates a replacement.
If the template contains a mistake, the replacement inherits it.

In the practical checkpoint, apply the supplied `web.yaml` inside the assigned
project. It declares an application image pinned by digest, one replica, bounded
CPU and memory, and the workload security settings required by the lab. Run
`oc apply -f web.yaml`, then inspect the resulting Deployment and pods. The lab
supplies the actual file and project; the text exercise does not create resources.
Do not strip security settings to work around an admission rejection.

A changed pod template starts a new rollout. Observe it with
`oc rollout status deployment/web --timeout=60s`. A timeout means it did not finish
within that window; inspect events and conditions before choosing a repair.
If the supplied broken update uses an invalid image, restore the approved digest
in the manifest and apply it again. An imperative `oc set image` change is also
valid when it produces the required safe final state. It can differ from the
saved file, so reconcile that file before future applies.

An older replica may keep serving while the new rollout is stuck. Therefore,
"one pod is Ready" is weaker evidence than "the latest Deployment generation has
been observed, the intended updated replicas are Ready, and the rollout finished."
Verify the new state, then verify the application's response.

The checkpoint first records a working deployment, then introduces a controlled
image mistake and records that failure before repair. This sequence gives trusted
evidence of recovery. A final healthy screenshot alone cannot prove the failure
was encountered and repaired. Reset starts a new lab generation and repeats the
sequence; it cannot reuse evidence from the old attempt.

entities.description: Trace a request through a Route and Service to a ready application pod.
entities.title: Connect a Service and Route

entities.explanation_markdown:
# Connect a Service and Route

Estimated time: 10 minutes, including four practice exercises.
Prerequisite: Deploy and repair a workload.

Pods can be replaced, so their addresses are not a stable application interface.
A Service supplies a stable in-cluster endpoint and selects backend pods by labels.
Its selector must match the intended pods. A similar resource name alone creates
no association. The Service port maps to a target port where the application
actually listens; declaring a container port does not start a listener.

For this lab, the web container listens on 8080. After deploying it, create a
ClusterIP Service with `oc expose deployment web --port=8080 --target-port=8080`.
Inspect it with `oc describe service web`. Confirm its selector and backend
readiness before blaming external routing. The platform maintains EndpointSlices
for Services; an empty ready backend set points you toward selection or readiness.

An OpenShift Route connects an external host at the ingress router to a Service.
Create the lab's edge-terminated Route with `oc create route edge web
--service=web --port=8080 --insecure-policy=Redirect`. This uses the router's
configured certificate; learners do not need to read or upload private keys.
TLS ends at the router, and this example forwards HTTP to the application.
Edge termination is not a claim of encryption on every internal hop.

Inspect the assigned Route host and its admission status. Then use an HTTPS
client with the trusted cluster certificate chain to request that host and check
the expected application response. A Route object or router error page is not
proof of success. Diagnose in order: current rollout, Service selector and target
port, Route target/admission, then the external response. Infrastructure DNS,
certificate or router failures require lab support rather than a learner penalty.

Your checkpoint outcome is a healthy current rollout and a reachable application,
including recovery from the controlled failure. It does not grant access to
cluster-wide network policy or complete the full DO180/DO280 curriculum.

entities.description: Apply a manifest change and verify the resulting desired and observed resource state.
entities.title: Apply and verify manifests

entities.explanation_markdown:
# Apply and verify manifests

Outcome: apply a manifest change and verify desired and observed resource state.
Allow about 12 minutes including four practice exercises. Complete foundations,
trusted checkpoint A, and YAML editing prerequisites first. This lesson is an
original, bounded DO280-aligned pilot slice, not complete course coverage.

A manifest records desired state. Its `apiVersion` and `kind` identify the API
resource, `metadata.name` identifies the object, and `spec` describes the intended
configuration. A Deployment controller reconciles its pod template and replica
count asynchronously. A successful API response does not establish readiness.

Read the project assigned by your lab and confirm `oc project -q`. Inspect
`oc get deployment web -o yaml` before changing it. Keep the supplied workload's
image digest, resource requests/limits, and security settings. Change only the
fields requested by the exercise. Run `oc apply -f web.yaml` in the assigned
project. YAML indentation is structural; a field at the wrong level can be
rejected or fail to express the intended configuration.

Use `oc rollout status deployment/web --timeout=60s` and inspect the resulting
Deployment. Verify the controller observed the latest generation and that the
updated and ready replicas match the desired count. A ready pod from an older
revision is insufficient evidence. On failure, inspect conditions and events;
network/API failures are infrastructure problems, not wrong learner answers.

`oc create` creates a new object and usually fails if it already exists. `oc apply`
can reconcile a previously applied object. Reapplying an unchanged file should
preserve its intended state. If you imperatively change a field that the file
still specifies differently, a later apply can restore the file's value. Record
intentional changes in the manifest and verify actual state after every update.

Checkpoint B accepts equivalent manifest layouts producing the requested state;
it does not grade YAML key order. The short command exercises deliberately use
literal command matching, so their prompt specifies the requested spelling.

Review: explain why “configured” and “latest rollout ready” are different claims.

Reference: [OpenShift 4.22 object management](https://github.com/openshift/openshift-docs/blob/enterprise-4.22/cli_reference/openshift_cli/developer-cli-commands.adoc).

entities.title: Grant scoped read access

entities.explanation_markdown:
# Grant scoped read access

Outcome: grant a supplied identity pod read access in one project and verify
allowed and denied actions. Estimate: 12 minutes and four exercises. Complete
`oc-declarative` first. This is namespace-scoped pilot practice, not cluster-wide
identity administration or complete DO280 training.

Authentication establishes an identity; authorization decides which operations
that identity may perform. A namespaced Role contains API groups, resources and
verbs. For core pods, the API group is the empty string, the resource is `pods`,
and a minimal reader needs `get` and `list`. No wildcard, secret read or mutation
permission is needed. A RoleBinding connects that Role to a specific subject.

The operator supplies the ServiceAccount `supplied-reader` in your assigned
project. You do not create its credentials. In a RoleBinding subject, use kind
`ServiceAccount`, the exact name and its supplied namespace. In `roleRef`, use
API group `rbac.authorization.k8s.io`, kind `Role` and the name of your reader
Role. Create both using manifests in the assigned project. Changing a binding's
`roleRef` requires replacement; do not assume an apply can mutate that field.

A Role alone grants nobody access. A correct Role with the wrong binding subject
also fails the task. Conversely, adding a narrow Role does not revoke permissions
from another binding: RBAC grants are additive. The trusted test checks effective
access, including negative cases, rather than accepting resource names alone.

`oc auth can-i delete pods` checks your current identity in the selected project.
It does not prove what `supplied-reader` can do. The trusted operator tests the
supplied identity separately: pod list succeeds, while pod deletion, secret
reads and cross-project pod lists are denied. Its short-lived credential stays
outside your terminal. Do not request impersonation or use administrator
credentials to make a learner command succeed.

The lab permits creating only grants that pass Kubernetes escalation checks.
Binding cluster-admin, reading secrets, issuing tokens and changing the outer
isolation controls remain outside the exercise. A timeout is not proof of denial:
a negative access test requires an authorization rejection.

Review: identify the Role, binding and exact subject, then name one allowed and
three denied operations that would demonstrate the requested boundary.

Reference: [OpenShift 4.22 RBAC](https://github.com/openshift/openshift-docs/blob/enterprise-4.22/authentication/using-rbac.adoc).

entities.description: Configure an exercise quota beneath an operator ceiling and explain an admission denial.
entities.title: Set and diagnose a resource budget

entities.explanation_markdown:
# Set and diagnose a resource budget

Outcome: configure an exercise quota within an operator ceiling and explain an
admission denial. Estimate: 12 minutes and four exercises. Complete `oc-rbac`
first. This is a small namespace-scoped administration exercise, not full
capacity planning or complete DO280 coverage.

A ResourceQuota limits aggregate usage in a namespace for the resources it names.
`spec.hard` describes the limits; `status.used` describes accounted usage. It does
not reserve capacity or ensure that a pod can be scheduled. CPU and memory
requests guide scheduling; limits bound container resource use. A LimitRange,
which can supply defaults or per-object constraints, is a different resource.

The operator owns `outer-budget`: 500m CPU and 512Mi memory requests, 1 CPU and
1Gi memory limits, and four pods. You cannot modify or delete it. The exercise
owns a separate quota named `exercise-budget`, with `hard.pods: "1"`. Both apply
at the same time: a second quota does not add capacity or override the first.

Apply your exercise quota, then inspect `oc describe resourcequota exercise-budget`.
Wait until its status reflects the intended hard limit. With one existing pod,
a request to create a second pod should fail with `exceeded quota` naming
`exercise-budget`. The controlled probe has valid security and resource fields,
so a different rejection is not evidence that this quota is correct.

A quota rejection can be reported as Forbidden even when the caller has RBAC
permission to create pods. Read the reason before changing permissions. Do not
solve the exercise by raising the outer ceiling, deleting isolation policies,
or adding a broader role. In real operations, reduce use or request an authorized
budget adjustment; here the assignment intentionally requires a one-pod quota.

A one-pod quota can prevent a rolling update that needs a temporary surge pod.
For checkpoint B, finish and verify the manifest update before imposing the
one-pod quota. During reset, the operator removes the exercise quota before
recreating the workload, while retaining the outer ceiling and isolation rules.
This ordering prevents an expected admission limit from masquerading as a broken
image or network error.

Review: explain why a quota of one plus a quota of four still rejects a second
pod, and distinguish that denial from RBAC denial and API unavailability.

Reference: [OpenShift 4.22 project quotas](https://github.com/openshift/openshift-docs/blob/enterprise-4.22/applications/quotas/quotas-setting-per-project.adoc).
